source.title: Localizing Task Recognition and Task Learning in In-Context Learning via Attention Head Analysis
source.authors: Hao-Lin Yang; Hakaze Cho; Naoya Inoue

record.tranche_reason: The study measures induction-head-like attention patterns and tests their role in in-context learning through head ablations, but uses its own head-identification and task-recognition/task-learning analyses rather than reproducing the original training-time emergence measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper defines and scores induction heads by attention to demonstration-label positions after earlier colons, measures their overlap and rankings relative to task-recognition/task-learning heads, and ablates induction heads while reporting accuracy and task-recognition ratio. It does not report induction-head formation over training, training-loss bumps, or token-index loss curves. Statements about prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study ablates heads it scores as induction heads in six pretrained LLMs (3B–34B) and measures classification ICL accuracy and task-recognition ratio. It argues these heads act mainly through label-space recognition rather than learning the text–label mapping, which restates their role in ICL (V3) and bears on V6. Caveat: its IH score is only attention from the final colon to the demonstration-label tokens. No prefix-matching or copying test on repeated tokens is run, so 'IH' here means label-attending heads.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that induction heads (defined by attention to demonstration-label tokens) are largely a subset of task-recognition heads. These heads help recognise the label space rather than selectively promote the correct label. Task-recognition and task-learning heads are distinct, complementary mechanisms of ICL.
record.recipe_differences: Identifies IHs using attention-pattern scores on classification prompts and relates them to TSLA-identified TR/TL heads; adds ranking analyses and head ablations. It does not reproduce training-time induction-head emergence or loss-curve measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The analysis uses a top 3% threshold for its main comparisons; it also examines other thresholds. The reported head rankings and ablation effects vary by model and dataset. IH identification uses attention at the final colon toward demonstration-label positions.

fits_no_version.finding: The top 3% label-attending ('IH') head sets are consistent across seven datasets within each model (Jaccard 0.43–0.48), more so than TL heads.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Heads scored as induction heads in ICL prompts are largely task-invariant within a model.

record.problems: The induction-head ablation plots do not provide exact values in the text. The IH identification is based on attention patterns and does not establish the full previous-token-head composition or directly measure copying. The ablation results are averaged across datasets in the main analysis, and the study does not measure training-time emergence or quantify the share of all ICL carried by IHs.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported results were left out. The paper also reports layer distributions, steering, and geometric analyses, but those results do not directly measure the claim versions about induction-head emergence, broad ICL contribution, or few-shot learning carriers.

untested.parts: Not tested: composition with a previous-token head, and [A][B]…[A]→[B] copying. IH identity is inferred only from attention to label tokens.
Not tested: no training dynamics, phase change or loss bump.
Not tested: loss falling with token index, the share of ICL carried, and non-classification ICL for IH ablation.
Not tested: the presence of induction behaviour across families, runs, architectures or modalities (no prefix-matching test).
Not tested: no variation in training data or setup.

missing.what: TR–IH vs TL–IH overlap, rank correlations and Conditional Mean Percentage for the five other models (V6 evidence beyond Llama3-8B)
TL-head ablation accuracy and TR ratio for the five other models
Mean layer of IHs vs TL vs TR heads with Mann–Whitney p-values: IHs sit in layers like TL heads, far shallower than TR heads

record.verdict_notes: IH scoring (Appendix E) sums the final-colon attention to the label tokens. No repeated-random-token prefix-matching test is used, so links to the canonical induction-head definition are indirect. The reader's V1 and V4 links were removed. Tranche changed to T5 because the paper argues IHs act through task recognition, restating their role in ICL.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test composition with an earlier previous-token head or directly test copying on the general [A][B] … [A] → [B] task; the analysis uses label-token attention in classification prompts.
No training-time emergence, narrow formation window, loss-curve bump, or token-index in-context-learning gain is measured.

Tests induction-head ablation effects on classification ICL accuracy and task-recognition ratio, but does not quantify what fraction of total ICL they carry, test loss falling with token index, or assess all large-transformer ICL tasks.
Tests induction-head-related patterns in six named model families/sizes; does not test multiple training runs, other architectures, or other modalities.
Does not vary pretraining data or training setup to test whether or when heads form, or whether ICL persists.

Tests the distinction between induction-head/task-recognition effects and task-learning-head effects in the reported classification settings; does not establish the main carrier of few-shot learning across all task types.
Does not examine training-time formation as one transition or multiple sub-steps.

rows.operation_detail: Compared top-ranked task-recognition, task-learning, and induction heads using overlap and ranking correlations.

rows.value: figure only; text says TR–IH overlap is much larger than TR–TL or TL–IH and significantly above random baseline, and TR–IH rank correlations are consistently higher
rows.note: Induction-head scores are based on attention-pattern resemblance to induction heads. This relates induction-head-like heads to task recognition but does not test their full circuit mechanism.
rows.check: Does not bear on V1: overlap with TR heads says nothing about previous-token composition or [A][B]…[A]→[B] copying. For V6, the low TL–IH overlap and correlation is the relevant result, so the state is observed rather than partial. The value is figure-only; the random Jaccard baseline of 0.0152 is stated in a footnote.

relationships.condition: 8-shot classification ICL (seven datasets), top 3% label-attending 'IH' heads, six models (Llama3/3.1/3.2, Qwen2/2.5, Yi)
relationships.reason: IH ablation causes large accuracy loss, but mainly because predictions leave the label set (failed task recognition). This places IHs' role in recognising the label space rather than in ICL as a whole (r3, r4, r12–r21).
relationships.display_finding: Ablation caused large accuracy losses mainly because predictions left the label set, tying these heads primarily to task recognition.

source_check.reason: Sections 4.1–4.2 and Appendix H.1 attribute IH-ablation losses primarily to failed label-space recognition, while separate TL heads contribute label discrimination. This qualifies the mechanism in the tested classification setting.

relationships.condition: Llama3-8B classification ICL, averaged over seven datasets
relationships.reason: IHs overlap little with TL heads and rank low in the TL ranking. IH ablation mostly destroys task recognition, while ablating the separate TL heads lowers accuracy about 30% with TR ratio down only about 10% (r1, r2, r3, r4, r5).
relationships.display_finding: Induction heads overlapped little with task-learning heads and mainly affected task recognition, while ablating task-learning heads lowered accuracy about 30% and reduced the task-recognition ratio about 10%.
